title: "FDA Inspection Authority and Outcomes"

## The knock on the door

An FDA (Food and Drug Administration) investigator is in Lakeshore's lobby. No surprise
phone call last night, no dramatic cold open — this is simply Lakeshore's turn. It's been
long enough since the last visit that a **routine** inspection was due, the same way a
periodic external audit comes around on its own schedule rather than because something
went wrong. Nothing has been reported, nothing has failed, nothing is on fire. The
investigator presents a federal credential and a written notice of inspection, and asks to
speak with the person in charge.

That's you, functionally, even though the Quality Analyst (QA) who reports to you will do
most of the walking and talking today. You already know, from `data-integrity-and-records`'s
own self-assessment, DI-0301, exactly what's sitting unresolved on your desk: DED-0458, a
donor-eligibility record that settled clean on four of ALCOA's five letters but still has a
genuinely open question on "accurate"; LAB-07, a legacy lab instrument with a real,
standing gap in its documented fitness-for-use justification; and a cumulative
deferred-donor record that's fully compliant with its "at least monthly" update floor, with
Lakeshore's own written policy on whether monthly is fast enough for its actual risk
tolerance still under internal review. None of that is secret from you. The question today
is whether any of it becomes something an investigator writes down.

You have about four hours before the investigator starts asking for specific records. This
module is what you need to know before that clock runs out: what the investigator can
actually walk in and demand, what's legally off-limits no matter how the conversation goes,
what the form at the end of the day actually means and doesn't mean, and the three ways
this particular visit can end.

## Why this rule exists — and the ITSM bridge

FDA's inspection authority exists because self-reported compliance isn't verification.
A blood establishment could write a perfect set of SOPs (standard operating procedures) and
still not follow a single one of them in practice. The only way to know whether a paper
quality system matches a real one is for someone with no stake in the answer to walk in,
look at the actual records, watch the actual process, and ask the actual people doing the
work. That's not a courtesy FDA extends. It's the entire reason the inspection power exists
in the first place: patient safety depends on practice matching documentation, and nobody
verifies their own homework reliably.

You already run something structurally identical. An external security or compliance audit
— SOC 2, PCI, an unannounced or lightly-announced vendor-risk review — works the same way.
An outside auditor with defined scope and defined authority shows up, asks to see specific
evidence (configuration exports, access logs, change records), and produces a findings
report at the end that you then have to respond to. An FDA inspection is that same shape,
with one real difference, and it's the difference this whole module is built around: your
external auditor's scope is usually negotiable — you agree on it in a kickoff call, and a
disputed finding can sometimes be argued down in a closing meeting. An FDA investigator's
scope is not a negotiation. It's set by federal statute, passed by Congress, and neither the
investigator nor you gets to redraw its boundaries on the spot. What's off-limits is
off-limits because the law says so, not because the inspector agreed to leave it alone.

## The rule in plain English

Here's what the law actually gives an FDA investigator, and what it withholds.

**What they can enter and inspect.** At reasonable times, an investigator can enter any
facility where regulated products — including blood and blood components — are
manufactured, processed, or held, and can inspect the facility itself, equipment, materials,
containers, and labeling. For an establishment like Lakeshore, inspection extends further:
to records, files, papers, processes, and controls — essentially anything bearing on
whether Lakeshore's products are being made and held the way the regulations require. This
is where BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software) records, SOPs, training files,
equipment logs, and maintenance history all become fair game. LAB-07's own fitness-for-use
documentation — or the hole where it should be — is exactly the kind of thing this reaches.

**What's off-limits, by law, not by courtesy.** The same statute draws an explicit line:
inspection does not reach financial data, sales data (other than shipment data), pricing
data, personnel data (except records of the technical qualifications of staff performing
regulated functions), or research data. An investigator can ask what training a phlebotomist
completed before drawing blood. An investigator cannot ask what that phlebotomist is paid,
or pull Lakeshore's internal budget memos.

**What a Form FDA 483 actually is — and isn't.** At the end of an inspection, if the
investigator's own judgment is that something observed indicates a possible violation, they
issue a written report of those observations. FDA's own administrative name for that report
is Form FDA 483. It is real, it is serious, and it is not a final verdict. It reflects one
investigator's judgment at one point in time, before Lakeshore's written response and before
any further review inside FDA. A 483 is an opening move in a conversation, not a conviction.

**The three possible outcomes.** Every FDA inspection — not just this one — ends in one of
three classifications: **NAI** (No Action Indicated — no violations found), **VAI**
(Voluntary Action Indicated — violations found, but not serious enough to warrant formal
action), or **OAI** (Official Action Indicated — serious, repeated, or deliberate
noncompliance that triggers a stronger FDA response). A 483 can lead to any of the three; it
is not itself the outcome.

**Routine versus for-cause — handled precisely, because the precision matters.** FDA field
staff genuinely distinguish between a **routine** inspection (scheduled as part of ordinary
surveillance, the way Lakeshore's is this time) and a **for-cause** inspection (triggered by
a specific complaint, adverse event report, or known problem). That distinction is real and
it matters operationally. But here's the trap worth naming now, before the common-traps
section: "for-cause inspection" is not a single, FDA-wide, legally defined term that governs
every industry FDA regulates. As the decoder table below shows, it appears as actual
statutory text in exactly one place — and that place is specific to medical device
establishments, not blood establishments, not drug manufacturers generally. Outside that one
device-specific subsection, "routine" and "for-cause" are FDA's own operational vocabulary —
real, used daily in the field, but administrative practice, not a universal statutory
category.

**One line to keep separate for later:** a Form 483 or an OAI finding is how FDA inspections
can escalate — that's module 2's subject, not this one. And an AABB (Association for the
Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) assessment is a completely different process — voluntary,
industry-run, checking Lakeshore against AABB's own Standards rather than federal law. Keep
the two apart; module 4 builds AABB's process out properly.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 U.S.C. 374(a)(1) | "Title twenty-one, Section three-seventy-four, subsection a, paragraph one" | **Statute.** Entry and inspection authority; what inspection may reach; the explicit financial/pricing/personnel/research-data carve-out. | What the investigator can walk in and demand to see at Lakeshore — and the hard boundary around it. |
| 21 U.S.C. 374(b)(1) | "Subsection b, paragraph one" | **Statute.** Requires a written report of observed conditions before the investigator leaves the premises, with a copy sent to FDA. | Form FDA 483's actual legal basis — the statute never uses the word "483," it says "a report in writing." |
| 21 U.S.C. 374(c) | "Subsection c" | **Statute.** If a sample was taken, a receipt describing it must be given before the investigator leaves. | Covers any physical sample the investigator might pull during today's visit. |
| 21 U.S.C. 374(h)(1), opening clause | "Subsection h, paragraph one" | **Statute**, device-establishment-specific (added 2017). The one place "for-cause inspection" is actual statutory language — and it isn't general. | The narrow textual anchor behind this module's routine-vs-for-cause nuance. |
| FDA, "Inspection Observations" (public page) | "FDA's inspection-observations page" | **FDA informational/administrative source**, not regulation or formal guidance. Describes what gets listed on a Form 483 and why. | Confirms a 483 reflects investigator judgment, not a final determination. |
| FDA, "CDER GCP Inspections and Outcomes" (2022), slide 12 | "the NAI/VAI/OAI slide" | **FDA informational source** (a GCP-specific presentation). The three-outcome classification scheme itself is general FDA-wide practice; the slide's own clinical-trial content is not. | Where today's inspection is headed — and the scope caveat you need to state honestly. |

## The actual text

21 U.S.C. 374(a)(1) — entry and inspection authority:

> officers or employees duly designated by the Secretary, upon presenting appropriate
> credentials and a written notice to the owner, operator, or agent in charge, are
> authorized (A) to enter, at reasonable times, any factory, warehouse, or establishment in
> which food, drugs, devices, tobacco products, or cosmetics are manufactured, processed,
> packed, or held... and (B) to inspect, at reasonable times and within reasonable limits
> and in a reasonable manner, such factory, warehouse, establishment, or vehicle and all
> pertinent equipment, finished and unfinished materials, containers, and labeling therein.

("The Secretary" is the statute's own language for the Secretary of Health and Human
Services, whose inspection authority is delegated down to FDA investigators in practice.)

The same subsection extends that reach further, and then draws its own line:

> the inspection shall extend to all things therein (including records, files, papers,
> processes, controls, and facilities) bearing on whether [the product] ... or otherwise
> bearing on violation of this chapter. No inspection authorized by the preceding sentence
> or by paragraph (3) shall extend to financial data, sales data other than shipment data,
> pricing data, personnel data (other than data as to qualification of technical and
> professional personnel performing functions subject to this chapter), and research data.

21 U.S.C. 374(b)(1) — the written report, Form 483's statutory basis:

> Upon completion of any such inspection ... and prior to leaving the premises, the officer
> or employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
> report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
> judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, tobacco product, or cosmetic in such
> establishment (A) consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed
> substance, or (B) has been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby
> it may have become contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious
> to health. A copy of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary.

Notice what that sentence does *not* say: it never says "Form FDA 483." The statute requires
"a report in writing." Form FDA 483 is FDA's own administrative instrument — a standardized
form — for fulfilling that statutory duty. The form is FDA's creation; the duty to issue
something in writing is Congress's.

21 U.S.C. 374(c) — sample receipts:

> If the officer or employee making any such inspection ... has obtained any sample in the
> course of the inspection, upon completion of the inspection and prior to leaving the
> premises he shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a receipt describing the
> samples obtained.

21 U.S.C. 374(h)(1), opening clause — the only place "for-cause inspection" is actual
statutory text, and it's narrow:

> In the case of inspections other than for-cause inspections, the Secretary shall review
> processes and standards applicable to inspections of domestic and foreign device
> establishments in effect as of August 18, 2017, and update such processes and standards
> through the adoption of uniform processes and standards applicable to such inspections.

That sentence is about FDA's own internal device-inspection program. It is not a definition
reaching blood establishments, drug manufacturers generally, or anything outside devices.

FDA's own description of Form 483, from its public "Inspection Observations" page
(**FDA informational/administrative source** — not a guidance document, not regulation):

> These observations are listed on an FDA Form 483 when, in an investigator's judgment, the
> observed conditions or practices indicate that an FDA-regulated product may be in
> violation of FDA's requirements.

The three post-inspection outcomes, from an FDA presentation on CDER's (Center for Drug
Evaluation and Research) GCP (Good Clinical Practice) inspections — **FDA informational
source**:

> NAI: no violations identified
>
> VAI: violations identified but do not meet the threshold for OAI
>
> OAI: serious noncompliance, repeated or deliberate failure to comply with the regulations

**The scope caveat, stated plainly:** that source is about a different kind of FDA
inspection entirely — GCP inspections of clinical drug trials, checking investigators and
sponsors running human studies, not CGMP (current good manufacturing practice) inspections of
a manufacturing or blood-collection facility like Lakeshore. None of that presentation's
clinical-trial-specific content — study-subject risk, sponsor obligations, its own statistics
— has anything to do with Lakeshore. What *does* transfer, honestly, is the three-letter
scheme itself: NAI, VAI, and OAI are FDA-wide classifications, used the same way across
every inspection program FDA runs, CGMP inspections of blood establishments included. The
label is general. The slide's own examples are not.

## What the Director should have ready, going in

The subject of today's inspection is Lakeshore, not you personally — but you're the one who
has to know, before the investigator finishes their first cup of coffee, whether Lakeshore
is ready to answer for itself.

- **Facility access and escort plan.** Someone (usually your QA) walks every area the
  investigator asks to see. No area gets quietly skipped, and no one improvises an answer
  they don't actually know.
- **BECS records, pulled and current.** Donor-eligibility determinations, audit trail
  exports, access-control lists — anything an investigator could reasonably ask for under
  374(a)(1)'s "records, files, papers, processes, controls" language. If DED-0458 comes up,
  know exactly where its "accurate" question stands and say so plainly rather than
  pretending it's resolved.
- **Equipment and instrument fitness-for-use files.** LAB-07's documented-fitness-for-use
  gap is a real, standing finding DI-0301 already surfaced internally. If the investigator
  asks for that documentation, the honest answer is that it's a known gap, already being
  worked — not a surprise you're discovering in the room.
- **A clear internal answer on what's off-limits, held calmly.** If a request strays toward
  financial, pricing, or personnel data, your QA should be able to say so professionally and
  point to the statutory carve-out, not argue or stonewall.
- **A designated single point of contact for records requests**, so nothing gets handed over
  twice, inconsistently, or by someone without the authority to decide what's responsive.

## Common traps

**"For-cause inspection" is a real, legally defined category that covers every industry FDA
regulates, including us.** Not quite. As 374(h)(1) itself shows, "for-cause inspection"
exists in the statute exactly once, and that subsection is written for device
establishments specifically, added to the law in 2017. Outside that one place, "routine" and
"for-cause" are FDA's own operational vocabulary — genuinely used, genuinely meaningful in
the field, but not a universal statutory or regulatory term that applies the same way across
every FDA-regulated industry. Lakeshore's inspection today is routine in the ordinary,
administrative sense of that word — not because any statute defines "routine" for blood
establishments.

**"A Form 483 means we failed the inspection."** No. A 483 is one investigator's written
judgment, issued before Lakeshore's response and before any further FDA review. FDA's own
description says the observations indicate a product "may be" in violation — not that it is.
A 483 can resolve to NAI's near neighbor (rare, since a 483 implies at least an observation),
to VAI, or, in serious cases, to OAI. Which one it becomes depends on severity, pattern, and
what happens next — not on the mere existence of the form.

## What this means for your job

- **Never let "we're due for an inspection" become a scramble.** A routine cycle is
  predictable by definition — the DI-0301 findings sitting on your desk should already be
  the first thing you check, not something you discover is relevant mid-inspection.
- **Brief your QA on the off-limits boundary before the investigator arrives, not during.**
  "Financial, pricing, personnel data (other than staff qualifications), and research data
  are outside inspection scope" is a sentence she should be able to say calmly, not look up.
- **Treat a known, documented gap — like LAB-07's — as a strength, not a liability, if it's
  already being worked.** An investigator who finds a gap Lakeshore already knew about and is
  actively addressing sees a functioning quality system. An investigator who finds a gap
  nobody mentioned sees a quality system that doesn't know its own condition.
- **Don't argue with a 483 in the room.** The written response process exists for a reason;
  a defensive reaction in the moment helps nobody and the form isn't negotiable the way an
  internal audit's severity rating sometimes is.
- **Ask your QA, afterward, to walk you through every observation letter by letter** — not
  just "did we get a 483," but exactly what each observation says, in the investigator's own
  words, before anyone drafts a response.

## The inspection, and where it's likely headed

The investigator spends the day with your QA: BECS screens, SOP binders, LAB-07's
maintenance log, training records. The financial and personnel-data boundary never actually
gets tested — nothing asked for comes close to it. Before leaving, the investigator hands
your QA a Form FDA 483 with two observations:

1. **No documented evidence of periodic fitness-for-use review** for a legacy laboratory
   instrument used in testing — the exact shape of LAB-07's own standing gap, independently
   rediscovered by an outside investigator rather than invented fresh today.
2. **An SOP revision was implemented at one site before its final Quality-unit approval
   signature was dated**, a smaller, generic documentation-timing gap, unrelated to any
   locked finding from earlier courses.

Two observations, neither involving contaminated product, falsified records, or patient
harm. Which of the three outcomes does this land in?

That question is genuinely open tonight, and it should stay that way rather than get forced
to a clean answer for the sake of ending this module tidily. Here's the Director's own
reasoned judgment, not a certainty: **probably VAI.** Both observations are real
documentation gaps, which rules out NAI — "no violations identified" doesn't fit a 483 with
two of them on it. But neither observation shows the pattern OAI requires: nothing here is
repeated, deliberate, or tied to product that reached a patient unsafely. A single
previously-known equipment-documentation gap and a single SOP-timing lapse look, on their
face, like exactly the kind of finding VAI exists for — real, worth a written response and
real corrective action, but not the kind of serious or repeated failure that escalates
further. That's a working hypothesis for tonight, not a verdict — the actual classification
is FDA's call, made after Lakeshore's written response, not yours to assign in advance.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA says, "FDA inspections are either routine or for-cause — that's a defined legal category that applies to us the same way it applies to a device manufacturer." Right or wrong?

Wrong, and this is the nuance this module exists to catch. "For-cause inspection" appears as
actual statutory language in exactly one place, 21 U.S.C. 374(h)(1) — and that subsection,
added in 2017, is written specifically for device establishments. It is not a general
statutory definition reaching blood establishments, drug manufacturers, or any other
industry FDA regulates. Outside that one device-specific subsection, "routine" and
"for-cause" are FDA's own operational, administrative vocabulary — real and meaningful in
day-to-day field practice, but not a single universally defined legal term. Today's
inspection is routine in that ordinary, administrative sense, not because a statute defines
"routine" for Lakeshore specifically.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: The investigator asks your QA what Lakeshore pays its phlebotomists per hour, as context for staffing levels. Does she have to answer?

No. 21 U.S.C. 374(a)(1)'s own carve-out excludes personnel data from inspection scope,
except for records of the technical and professional qualifications of staff performing
regulated functions. Pay rates are personnel data, not qualifications data. A professional,
calm response — pointing to the statutory boundary — is appropriate. It isn't
obstruction; it's exactly what the law itself withholds from inspection.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Is the NAI/VAI/OAI classification scheme itself a blood-establishment-specific or CGMP-specific regulation?

No — and this is **not a regulation at all** in the formal sense, nor is it specific to
blood establishments. The verified source for it is an FDA presentation about GCP
(Good Clinical Practice) inspections of clinical drug trials, an entirely different
inspection program. But the three-letter classification scheme itself — NAI, VAI, OAI — is
general FDA-wide administrative practice, used the same way across every kind of FDA
inspection, CGMP inspections of blood establishments included. What doesn't transfer from
that source is its own clinical-trial-specific content — subject risk, sponsor obligations,
its statistics — none of which has any bearing on Lakeshore's inspection.
:::

## Where this goes next

Lakeshore has its 483. Two honest, documented observations, no patient harm, a Director's
reasoned best guess of VAI that isn't yet a certainty. `warning-letters-and-recalls` picks up
from here: when a 483 — or a worse outcome — escalates into a Warning Letter, what that
